chief_complaint: acute confusion, staggering unsteadiness, and double vision over 3 days
hpi_details: 56-year-old male brought to emergency department by his brother due to acute, rapid deterioration over 3 days featuring severe confusion, staggering unsteadiness, and visual disturbances. Brother reports patient lives alone, has severe alcohol use disorder drinking 1 large bottle of vodka daily for years, and has eaten virtually no solid food for the past 3 weeks following a relationship breakdown. On arrival, patient is disoriented to time and place, muttering and confabulating details when asked where he is. When attempting to walk across the room, exhibits severe wide-based truncal ataxia, requiring two nurses to prevent falling. Complains of double vision when looking to the sides.
ideas: brother thinks he is just severely intoxicated or having alcohol withdrawal delirium (DTs)
concerns: brother is terrified he has suffered a permanent brain stroke from falling while drunk
expectations: wants IV rehydration fluids, glucose drip to clear the alcohol, and a brain scan
pmh: severe chronic alcohol dependence, alcohol-related liver disease, chronic malnutrition
social_hx: chronic heavy vodka intake (250-300g/day), unemployed, lives alone in neglected flat, severe dietary neglect

investigation_events.title: Emergency glucose and electrolyte assessment
investigation_events.availability_message: Point-of-care glucose and urgent electrolyte results are now available. Parenteral thiamine should be given promptly and must not be delayed for these results.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Acute Wernicke's Encephalopathy evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Acute Wernicke's Encephalopathy is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes Medical emergency: immediately administer high-dose Intravenous Thiamine (Pabrinex 2 pairs of ampoules IV three times daily diluted in 100 mL normal saline over 30 minutes for 3 to 5 days), adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: acute confusion, staggering unsteadiness, and double vision over 3 days

Key HPI features: 56-year-old male brought to emergency department by his brother due to acute, rapid deterioration over 3 days featuring severe confusion, staggering unsteadiness, and visual disturbances. Brother reports patient lives alone, has severe alcohol use disorder drinking 1 large bottle of vodka daily for years, and has eaten virtually no solid food for the past 3 weeks following a relationship breakdown. On arrival, patient is disoriented to time and place, muttering and confabulating details when asked where he is. When attempting to walk across the room, exhibits severe wide-based truncal ataxia, requiring two nurses to prevent falling. Complains of double vision when looking to the sides.

Objective/Exam findings: Perform targeted neurological exam identifying the classical Wernicke Triad. 1. Ophthalmoplegia/Ocular signs: bilateral horizontal nystagmus on gaze testing, bilateral lateral rectus weakness (cranial nerve VI palsy causing horizontal diplopia), conjugate gaze palsies, and sluggish pupils. 2. Cerebellar/Gait Ataxia: severe broad-based truncal ataxia, unable to stand or perform heel-to-shin testing without losing balance. 3. Encephalopathy: global disorientation, apathy, and confabulation. Check vitals (hypothermia and postural hypotension common). CRITICAL EMERGENCY LAB PROTOCOL: check capillary blood glucose. NEVER ADMINISTER IV GLUCOSE OR DEXTROSE INFUSIONS PRIOR TO THIAMINE REPLACEMENT (giving glucose to a thiamine-deficient brain rapidly depletes remaining pyrophosphate cofactor stores, precipitating irreversible neuronal death and acute Korsakoff psychosis). Bloods: FBC, U&Es, LFTs, magnesium (hypomagnesaemia impairs thiamine utilization and must be corrected simultaneously), phosphate, clotting. MRI Brain (T2/FLAIR shows hyperintensities and petechial haemorrhages in the mammillary bodies, periaqueductal grey matter, medial thalami, and floor of 3rd/4th ventricles).
Relevant background/PMH: severe chronic alcohol dependence, alcohol-related liver disease, chronic malnutrition
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Acute Wernicke's Encephalopathy.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Hepatic encephalopathy without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Any glucose given before thiamine — can precipitate or worsen Wernicke's encephalopathy.
management_principles: Medical emergency: immediately administer high-dose Intravenous Thiamine (Pabrinex 2 pairs of ampoules IV three times daily diluted in 100 mL normal saline over 30 minutes for 3 to 5 days)
Administer IV thiamine BEFORE or co-administered with any IV glucose/crystalloid fluids
Correct concomitant hypomagnesaemia and electrolyte disturbances
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.assessment: Acute Wernicke's Encephalopathy secondary to severe thiamine (Vitamin B1) deficiency. DDx: hepatic encephalopathy (shows asterixis/flapping tremor, elevated ammonia), alcohol withdrawal delirium / Delirium Tremens (shows profound autonomic hyperactivity, tachycardia, hypertension, visual hallucinations), acute cerebellar/brainstem stroke, basilar artery occlusion, hypoglycaemia.
reference_soap.plan: This is a medical emergency requiring immediate hospital treatment. Give parenteral thiamine promptly, ideally before or alongside carbohydrate administration; do not delay treatment of hypoglycaemia. Correct magnesium and other electrolyte abnormalities, monitor neurologic status, and involve alcohol-dependence and nutrition services.

learning_objectives: Identify the classical Wernicke's clinical triad: acute encephalopathy, ocular abnormalities (nystagmus/VIth nerve palsy), and gait ataxia
Execute the absolute life-saving pharmacological rule: administer high-dose IV thiamine (Pabrinex) BEFORE or with any IV glucose administration
Explain the biochemical mechanism whereby glucose infusion without thiamine cofactor depletes brain pyrophosphate and triggers neuronal necrosis
Recognise the mandatory requirement to correct hypomagnesaemia simultaneously to enable enzymatic thiamine pyrophosphate utilization

teaching.one_liner: Severe thiamine (Vitamin B1) deficiency, from chronic alcohol use and poor nutrition, causes the classic triad of confusion, unsteady walking, and eye movement abnormalities — a medical emergency treated with IV thiamine before any glucose, since glucose alone can precipitate the crisis.
red_flags: Any glucose given before thiamine — can precipitate or worsen Wernicke's encephalopathy

must_ask.say: How much alcohol has he been drinking, and has he been eating regularly?
How confused is he — does he know where he is?
How steady is he when walking?
Any double vision or abnormal eye movements?
How many days has this deterioration been happening?

history.answer: My brother has gotten terribly confused and unsteady on his feet over the past three days, and he told me he has been seeing double.
Before three days ago, his memory and thinking were completely normal for him, and he took care of all his own daily chores.
It started about three days ago and has gotten steadily worse each day without any periods of clearing up.
He seems very drowsy and slow to answer, and he has no idea what day it is or that we are at a hospital.
He isn't seeing bugs or shadows, but when I ask him what he did today, he makes up stories that he was out working.
I checked his head and didn't see any bruises or cuts from falls, and he doesn't take any blood-thinning pills.
He can move both arms and legs equally and his face isn't drooping, though his words sound a bit slow and muttered.
He hasn't complained of any headache, and he hasn't thrown up at all.
No, he has never had any shaking fits, blank staring spells, or loss of bladder control.
No fever, no cough, and his urine looks normal without any foul smell or pain.
His neck moves easily without any stiffness, and bright room lights don't bother his eyes.
He does not have diabetes, doesn't take insulin or sugar pills, and hasn't complained of extreme thirst.
He hasn't eaten any solid food for almost three weeks since his partner left him, surviving only on alcohol and tap water.
He hasn't started any new sleeping pills, painkillers, or prescription medications.
He drinks about one large bottle of vodka every single day, and his last drink was earlier this morning.
He started staggering three days ago like a sailor on a rocking boat, and today he couldn't stand up without two people holding him.
He said things look doubled side-by-side whenever he looks to the left or right, but he has no eye pain.
He lives alone with electric heating, and no one else around him has been sick or exposed to fumes or chemicals.
A doctor told him years ago he had alcohol-related liver trouble, but his belly isn't swollen and his skin hasn't turned bright yellow.
He has never had psychiatric hospitalizations, mania, or severe depression before, just a long struggle with alcohol.
I thought he might just be heavily intoxicated or having the DTs from drinking so heavily.
I'm terrified that he might have suffered a permanent brain stroke after losing his balance.
I was hoping you could give him IV fluids and a glucose drip to flush the alcohol, and get a brain scan.
He has chronic alcohol dependence, alcoholic liver disease, and long-standing malnutrition, but no high blood pressure or heart disease.
He had his appendix removed in his twenties, but he hasn't had any recent hospital stays.
He takes no regular medications, no vitamins, and no health supplements.
He has no known allergies to any medications or foods.
He has smoked about one pack of cigarettes a day for thirty years.
He is currently unemployed and lives alone in an apartment that has become quite neglected.
Our father had high blood pressure and an alcohol problem, but there is no family history of early stroke or dementia.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 100/62 mmHg, heart rate 78 beats/min, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, temperature 35.8 °C, oxygen saturation 98% on room air; fingerstick blood glucose is 62 mg/dL.
Disheveled, emaciated middle-aged male lying in bed, appearing lethargic and undernourished, with no visible scalp lacerations or hematomas.
Mild icteric tinge to the sclerae bilaterally; conjunctivae are slightly pale without subconjunctival hemorrhages.
Pupils are equal but sluggish to light bilaterally; bilateral lateral rectus weakness with impaired lateral abduction and prominent horizontal nystagmus on lateral gaze.
Oral mucosa is dry with a noticeable stale alcohol odor; tongue and oral cavity show no bite marks or lacerations.
Drowsy and slow to respond, disoriented to time and place, displaying marked apathy and confabulating about recent events.
Generalized muscle wasting throughout, symmetric tone, motor strength 5/5 in all four extremities with no focal weakness or asymmetry.
Severe wide-based truncal ataxia, unable to maintain upright balance or walk unassisted, with bilaterally dysmetric heel-to-shin testing.
Fine intention tremor noted on finger approach, but asterixis and resting tremors are absent.
Neck is supple with full passive flexion, and both Kernig and Brudzinski signs are negative.
